sources.title: Barberena and colleagues, Multi-isotopic and morphometric evidence for the migration of farmers leading up to the Inka conquest of the southern Andes (2020)
sources.note: Direct original paper read selectively, Introduction on southern-Andean economic diversity and domestic/wild foods. Used only for regional context. Its specific migration interpretation is not repeated; the newer 2026 genomic paper supplies local transition and migration claims.

sources.title: Fernando Franchetti and Nuria Sugrañes, Ceramic technology, environment & residential mobility in small scale groups (2012)
sources.note: Direct original Before Farming 2012/3 article 2 PDF read: pages 2 to 3 regional water and seasonal movements, pages 5 to 6 El Indígeno and assemblages, pages 8 to 9 interpretation and chronological limits. Studies southern Mendoza, not all Andes. No pottery-equals-farming inference. Source comparisons are not exactly contemporaneous.

sources.title: Barberena and colleagues, Perspectivas arqueológicas para Patagonia Septentrional: Sitio Cueva Huenul 1 (2015)
sources.note: Direct original Magallania 43(1) paper read: chronology, lithic technology, discussion of Component 4. Late component assigned approximately last 1,600 years in paper; plant layers and small hearth/oven features, guanaco and tool maintenance supported. Older proposed rock-art chronology is superseded and not adopted.

sources.title: Llano, Sosa, Sánchez Campoo and Barberena, Arqueobotánica de Cueva Huenul 1 (2019)
sources.note: Original institutional PDF indexed abstract and printed pages 216 to 219 checked. Direct PDF fetch times out. Reproducible queries: "Arqueobotánica de Cueva Huenul 1" "Prosopis" "Holoceno tardío" and exact title "harina". Late-Holocene plant diversity and suggested summer occupation supported; anomalous maize in an early layer is not used to claim early cultivation.

sources.title: Local agricultural transition, crisis and migration in the Southern Andes, Nature 653 (2026), 124 to 133
sources.note: Direct publisher abstract and figure captions read; main full article not exposed in retrieved page. Published 18 March 2026. Abstract supports 46 newly sequenced genomes, local continuity across adoption of agriculture, migrants circa 810 to 700 calibrated years BP, probable matrilineal family movement, stress markers and pathogen-confirmed tuberculosis. All public claims bounded to abstract.

sources.title: Guadalupe Romero Villanueva, El arte rupestre de Cueva Huenul 1: un lugar persistente del noroeste de Patagonia (2022)
sources.note: Direct original Estudios Atacameños article read: morphology, techniques, colors, Discussion and Figure 9. Portable decorated materials dated broadly Late Holocene; one support directly dated 1,279 to 1,366 calibrated years BP. Record describes visual communication, not a deciphered language. Preliminary older mural chronology is not adopted because 2024 work revised direct dates.

sources.title: Biblioteca Nacional de Chile, Pehuenches y Puelches
sources.note: Direct national-library historical synthesis read: presentation on contact-period shelter/family leadership, colonial horses/exchange, later land alienation and continuing communities. Applied only to named Pehuenche communities, not prehistoric populations. Combined work budget includes the linked Pehuén capsule. Do not use erroneous 1992 law date or conflicting 1882/1883 fort chronology on page.

proposedOverrides.name: Andean hunter-gatherers
proposedOverrides.summary: An atlas umbrella spanning changing Chilean and Argentine landscapes, illustrated through local foraging archaeology, changing food economies and later distinct communities.

batchIdentityNotes.identity: Broad atlas subsistence label, not one archaeological culture, language, people or polity. Exact ID only, no aliases.
batchIdentityNotes.geometry: Early polygon spans approximately 18.31 to 41.79 degrees south, chiefly Chile and western Argentina. Later polygons contract southward after 1500 and inland after 1650. Actual manifest seams omit 1492 to 1500 and end at 1783 despite the index ending 1800. These are unresolved atlas coverage limits, not population disappearance.
batchIdentityNotes.pointEvidence: Cueva Huenul 1, Uspallata, Llancanelo, Malargüe and Lonquimay tested against decoded early, 1000 and 1500 polygons: all inside. Uspallata and Lonquimay fall outside the contracted 1650 and 1715 polygons; Huenul, Llancanelo and Malargüe remain inside. Later Pehuenche narrative is regional context and does not assert that the outline exactly contains their territory.
batchIdentityNotes.relations: Chinchorro, later Andean states, Mapuche and living Pehuenche identities are not absorbed as aliases. Named archaeological sites supply local examples without presumed ethnic descent. Pampas cultures remains distinct.
batchIdentityNotes.chronology: Examples emphasize late-Holocene evidence within the imported interval. Uspallata farming/migrant populations explicitly illustrate change beyond foraging. Portable art chronology uses the directly dated support, not the much earlier comb-shaped wall paintings whose chronology was revised in 2024. No artificial point years. BP conversions are approximate narrative ranges, not assigned radiocarbon construction dates.
batchIdentityNotes.evidenceLimits: No common native writing, invented sample, universal household, school, medical treatment or toilet system. Visual communication is distinguished from deciphered text. Disease evidence is restricted to the later studied Uspallata farming population; horse and piñón history restricted to named later Pehuenche communities.
